Before: Federated learning trains a shared model without pooling raw electronic health record (EHR) access logs. The server can still inspect individual model updates. This study compared detection performance and training cost with and without secure aggregation to protect those updates. It evaluated pooled centralised training, standard Federated Averaging and Federated Averaging with Secure Aggregation Plus (SecAgg+) using a long short-term memory autoencoder, a model that learns to reconstruct routine access sequences. Experiments used one supplied benchmark described as synthetic, three simulated clients and five random seeds. Sampling either retained the original client distributions or favoured selected departments. On the primary test, the mean paired differences in global average precision, a measure of threat ranking, between SecAgg+ and standard Federated Averaging were +0.0047 and +0.0001 in the two sampling conditions. These differences did not establish equivalent performance. Federated training did not consistently outperform pooled training. Compared with standard Federated Averaging, SecAgg+ increased the time recorded for the training workflow by 132.8% and 128.6%, respectively. The content carried in application messages increased by approximately 49.9%. All configurations struggled with unusual legitimate activity. SecAgg+ mean false-positive rates were 98.58% and 96.40% on the secondary test. Repeating the experiment in a fresh software environment on the same computer reproduced the predictions, with a disclosed exception in scaler metadata. Protected aggregation therefore added workflow cost without a clear detection benefit in this benchmark. Protection depended on a trusted host and honest participants. Incomplete records of data generation and the use of simulated clients limit what the findings imply for hospitals.
